clinicalPearls: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour that secretes pancreatic polypeptide but, because this hormone produces no distinctive clinical syndrome, behaves essentially as a non-functioning tumour
Frequently presents late with mass-effect features such as abdominal pain, obstructive jaundice, weight loss or a palpable mass, or is found incidentally on imaging
Most commonly located in the head or uncinate process of the pancreas, where pancreatic polypeptide cells are concentrated
A substantial proportion are malignant, with nodal or hepatic metastases at diagnosis, so it should not be assumed to be benign
Raised plasma pancreatic polypeptide is a useful biochemical marker and can aid MEN1 surveillance, but is not specific and rises in other conditions
Chromogranin A is a more general marker of neuroendocrine tumour burden and is used for monitoring
These tumours usually express somatostatin receptors, so somatostatin receptor PET/CT is valuable for localisation and staging

Management mirrors that of non-functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours: resection for localised disease, and somatostatin analogues, targeted agents, peptide receptor radionuclide therapy or chemotherapy for advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Pancreatic polypeptidoma is a well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour arising from pancreatic polypeptide (F) cells, which are concentrated in the head and uncinate process. Although the tumour oversecretes pancreatic polypeptide, this hormone does not generate a recognisable clinical syndrome, so the tumour is grouped clinically with non-functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and typically declares itself through local growth or metastasis rather than a hormonal effect. Elevated circulating pancreatic polypeptide therefore serves chiefly as a biochemical marker. As with other pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, tumorigenesis may be sporadic or occur within MEN1 through loss of menin, and behaviour is graded by proliferative activity.
additionalDifferentials: Non-functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour of other cell types
Other functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (gastrinoma, glucagonoma, VIPoma, somatostatinoma)
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Pancreatic metastasis from another primary such as renal cell carcinoma
Reactive or physiological elevation of pancreatic polypeptide
additionalInvestigations: Chromogranin A for tumour burden and monitoring
Multiphase contrast CT or MRI of the pancreas
Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration or biopsy for tissue and grading
Histological grading with Ki-67 proliferation index per WHO classification
MEN1 genetic testing and biochemical screening where indicated
redFlags: Obstructive jaundice or gastric outlet obstruction from a pancreatic head mass
Rapid weight loss or a rapidly enlarging mass
Hepatic or nodal metastases at presentation
High-grade histology with an elevated Ki-67 index
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on tumour grade and stage: localised, well-differentiated tumours resected completely have a favourable outlook, whereas high-grade or metastatic disease carries a worse prognosis, though often a more indolent course than pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
pitfalls: Interpreting a raised pancreatic polypeptide as diagnostic when it is non-specific and rises in other conditions
Mistaking the tumour for pancreatic adenocarcinoma and withholding appropriate neuroendocrine-directed therapy
Assuming non-functioning implies benign, thereby underestimating malignant potential
Omitting Ki-67 grading, which is central to prognosis and treatment selection
Failing to consider MEN1 in younger patients or those with other endocrine tumours
references: ENETS Consensus Guidelines for non-functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours: Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: Complete surgical resection as the mainstay for localised, well-differentiated tumours, by pancreaticoduodenectomy given the head or uncinate location, or enucleation for small lesions
Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or lanreotide for antiproliferative control of unresectable or metastatic well-differentiated disease
Further systemic options for progressive advanced disease including everolimus, sunitinib, peptide receptor radionuclide therapy with radiolabelled DOTATATE, or chemotherapy
Directed treatment of hepatic metastases by resection, ablation or embolisation where appropriate
Biochemical and imaging surveillance with plasma pancreatic polypeptide and chromogranin A alongside cross-sectional and somatostatin-receptor imaging
Screen for MEN1 with genetic counselling and family screening where indicated
Management within a specialist neuroendocrine tumour multidisciplinary team
